author: Ryan Burge
title: How the Graphs Get Made
summary: A behind-the-scenes look at how I turn data, code, writing, and AI into two newsletters every week
full_content:
I post something every Monday and Thursday on my newsletter. That’s been my cadence since nearly the beginning of this whole enterprise, and I like it very much. I think that’s the right rhythm for both me as an author and you as an audience. But it also means that I have to post something on Thanksgiving every year, because that always falls on a Thursday.

Instead of hitting you over the head with charts and graphs while you are worried about the right time and temperature for your turkey or whether you call it stuffing or dressing, I want to pull back the curtain a little bit on how the sausage is made at Graphs about Religion. It’s not something that I’ve ever done before, but I do get asked every once in a while about my writing process.

So, let me take you behind the scenes just a little bit on how all that happens.

The Idea

Okay, so I have to admit that this is easily the hardest process to describe because I really don’t know where all of the ideas come from and I do have a bit of existential dread that I will run out of good things to analyze. I honestly can’t pinpoint where the “seed” of a post emerges. I’ve always really resonated with the words of the iconic music producer Quincy Jones who said, “You’ve got to leave space for God to walk through the room.” And I really do believe that inspiration is something otherworldly. I used to show my students a TED Talk from Elizabeth Gilbert about “your elusive creative genius” that still resonates with me.

But it’s not an entirely free-wheeling process. There’s actually a lot of structure that hides behind the scenes. One thing that hardly anyone knows about is that I’ve been leveraging Claude and ChatGPT to build me a publishing pipeline website that I spend way too much time tweaking and upgrading, but it really is the framework for how this whole process works.

The website is only available to me, but I can log in anywhere in the world and it lays out my publishing schedule in a calendar format. I’m writing this post in mid-August and my next open slot for an article is November 5. I build my writing runway way out into the future. I often have 20 posts fully complete. You can see in the above screenshot that I already have a couple of slots already full for November.

The reason that the calendar view is so helpful is because I have a pretty clear cadence. Every Monday post is free for everyone. On two Thursdays a month, I write using data from the Association of Religion Data Archives and the rest of the Thursdays are posts only for my paid subscribers. That gives me some guard rails that help focus on my creativity. A Monday post is different from a paid Thursday one.

The Graphs

My ideas are always rooted in data. I don’t start by asking what questions I am interested in, I start by asking: what interesting questions can I answer with the data that I have available to me? Usually I am just mucking about with data sets that have been collected by other folks like the General Social Survey or the Cooperative Election Study. But more and more I have been trying to branch out and write about AA meetings in churches or how many polling places are located in houses of worship. That requires a data collection step before I can even get to the graphs.

Okay, so let’s say I have the data in hand. How do I make all those charts and graphs and maps that you see on a typical post? The answer is a piece of free and open source software called R. It was designed specifically for data analysis in mind but it has a very steep learning curve. There’s a whole story of how I taught myself to code in R that I don’t have time to share here, but I will mention this: I did not learn this skill in graduate school.

In the screenshot above you see what my desktop typically looks like. Hardly anyone uses base R to code in, instead we have an IDE that sits on top of R and gives us all kinds of functions and abilities to make it work faster and better. I’m partial to RStudio. I’ve tried Positron before, but it only makes my work harder without any real benefits. So I am sticking with old reliable for the time being.

I usually spend a couple of hours building graphs that will make up the backbone of the post. I say, without any sense of guilt, that this is where I lean on Claude and ChatGPT a whole lot. I have fed both of those systems tens of thousands of lines of code that I wrote long before AI was ubiquitous. So it knows my coding and graphing style. I can just say things like, “Okay, let’s calculate religious attendance by both age and gender,” and within ten seconds it’s produced a dozen lines of code that perfectly replicates what I would have done in a couple of minutes.

One thing that makes all of that more “custom” to me is that I have written a software package for R called socsci that contains a bundle of functions that are perfectly designed for my workflow. I built that package long before Artificial Intelligence came around (my first push was 7 years ago) but now Claude has helped me refine those functions and make them better. I wouldn’t know how to do data analysis without socsci riding along.

I keep all those graphs organized through a site that AI helped me build. It houses over 10,000 of my data visualizations. I had Claude run OCR on all these graphs so they are searchable and have been auto-tagged by the algorithm. So, if I want to quickly pull up a graph about Catholic attendance, it’s just a short query away.

The Writing

At this point, I take 5-6 of the graphs that I generated in the prior step and move them into a blank Google Doc. (By the way, type doc.new into a browser and be amazed). I call this “wireframing.” It just lays out what I think the narrative arc is going to be around the piece. A general rule of thumb is: start broad and go narrow. That’s how journal articles are laid out and it also makes the most sense for Substack, too. This is usually the point where I take a break. I walk away from the computer for a bit. I do some chores around the house, watch some TV, or run errands. I need to separate myself from the post for a while because in my head I’m formulating how I write the post.

Then, after I feel like I’ve ruminated on it enough, I sit back down at the keyboard and start to write. This is the part that goes the fastest. I’ve been known to write a complete 1,800 word draft in less than 60 minutes. I type very quickly and I know exactly what I want to say before I even sit down. I’m not trying to figure out the “beats” of the piece while I’m typing. I already have those in my head from the rumination phase. I just dump my thoughts out in a big rush. I bet that 95% of what I type during these sessions make it to the final published article.

After that, I’m usually pretty mentally spent. I need a break after an hour of intense focus. So, I walk away again. This time it’s only for an hour or two. I think through my argument again. I try to make sure it makes logical sense and that the narrative flows well. Then, I give AI this simple prompt: “I want you to clean up my writing. Don’t mess with my tone or style. Don’t try to condense anything. Just focus on grammar, spelling, syntax, etc.” That prompt is absolutely essential because if I don’t put those guardrails on the AI, it will try to grind down my voice into slop. I’ve found this to be incredibly effective at doing what I need it to do. I just want to fix my obvious mistakes. Nothing more or less.

Queuing it Up and Sending it Out

This part isn’t that exciting, really. It’s a whole bunch of drudgery and tedium. I’ve tried to find dozens of ways to make it go faster but I just can’t find a way to optimize this part. Here’s what happens next.

I move the post over to Substack. That’s pretty simple, usually. I literally just copy the whole post on Google Docs and paste it into the Substack platform. Then, I go through the piece paragraph by paragraph and bold some of the key sentences I think that readers who are just skimming my post need to focus on. It helps break up the “wall of text” feeling that can often happen.

Title, Subtitle, and Cover Image. This is where AI comes back into the discussion. I paste the full text of the piece into GPT, Claude and Gemini. I ask each of them to generate some title options. They usually each spit out about five of them. Most of those are similar to each other. I don’t spend too much time picking one out. I usually grab the one that pops off the screen immediately. Then I do the same thing for subtitles. But I ask this one to be descriptive and ideal for Search Engine Optimization so that a Google search will pick it up later on.

Finally, I use Gemini exclusively for the process of cover image generation. I’ve already fed it the full text of the post. I let Gemini know which title that I’ve settled on. Then I tell it to build a bright, colorful, dynamic image that is eye-catching for a Substack post. I tend to lean more towards cartoonish outputs or an infographic style. I then download it and copy it both to the Substack platform but also my “pipeline” website which I described earlier.

The Voice Over. I already have a couple of good microphones laying around my house because of all the podcasts I’ve done over the years, so I use one of those to capture me reading the text of each post. The program I use to record the audio and tweak it just a bit is called Audacity. It’s free and open source and just works really well. I don’t see any reason to switch to anything else.

I do actually read each of these, by the way. I could let AI do this pretty easily. I have hundreds of hours of my voice recorded through sermons, podcasts, and voice overs. So it wouldn’t be hard to train a model, but I still like the process of reading each of my articles into a microphone.

There’s a practical reason for doing it this way. It gives me one last chance to proofread and clean up my copy before it goes out into the world. This is the step when I realize if AI has taken away my voice because I will start stumbling over the words on the page because they aren’t my words. When I read my own words out loud, I know what is coming next. With AI, it just feels like someone else.

Scheduling the post. This is where the pipeline dashboard comes in handy. I look up what date I have open, I enter that information into the publishing screen and I set the time to send the piece out as 6:30AM central time. And then I’m done. I just have to do that 103 more times and I’ve filled up a year’s worth of calendar.

I hope that was interesting and informative for a lot of you who wonder what goes on behind the scenes of Graphs about Religion. I’m just a one man band and this is how I’ve made this process work for me. There’s no “right” way to do something like this. You make it up as you go along.

On this day of Thanksgiving, I am deeply thankful that anyone finds my work worth reading and sharing. It’s a gift that I don’t take lightly.

Ryan P. Burge is a professor of practice at the Danforth Center on Religion and Politics at Washington University.
